# Geometric Deep Learning

A Mathematical Perspective

Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges

Jorge Muñoz Fuentes

[gdl.fractalmanifold.com](https://gdl.fractalmanifold.com)

September 5, 2026

# Abstract

Deep learning has transformed artificial intelligence, yet traditional architectures are constrained to data with regular Euclidean structure (sequences, grids, voxels). Geometric Deep Learning (GDL) emerges as a unifying paradigm that extends these techniques to non-Euclidean domains—graphs, manifolds, groups—through the systematic incorporation of geometric symmetries. This book presents a rigorous mathematical analysis of GDL organized around the “5 Gs” framework: Geometry, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges.

The development begins with the formalization of classical neural networks using Lebesgue measure theory, including a complete proof of Cybenko’s universal approximation theorem. The GDL framework is built around the five Gs: Geometry provides the structure of data domains through Riemannian manifolds, tangent spaces, and curvature; Groups formalize symmetries via Lie groups and algebras, representation theory (Peter-Weyl and Schur theorems), and the equivariance principle; Graphs discretize continuous domains through spectral analysis and the graph Laplacian; Geodesics provide Riemannian metrics, the exponential map, and parallel transport for information propagation; and Gauges introduce local invariances through principal bundles and connections. This mathematical apparatus is applied to the formalization of equivariant convolutional networks—over finite groups, compact and non-compact Lie groups, and manifolds—and geometric attention mechanisms, including equivariant Transformers and hyperbolic attention.

Through formal proofs and detailed analyses, this book shows how fundamental geometric principles—equivariance, invariance, locality—unify convolutional networks, graph networks, and Transformers under a common geometric message passing framework. The result is a view of GDL as a mathematical framework that not only explains existing architectures but guides the design of new ones.

**Keywords**: Geometric Deep Learning, Group Theory, Equivariance, Riemannian Manifolds, Representation Theory, Lie Groups, Convolutional Networks, Graph Neural Networks, Transformers, Message Passing

## Preface

## Why this book

Most introductions to geometric deep learning start from the architectures. They present a convolutional network, then a graph network, then a transformer, and explain afterwards that each of them respects some symmetry of its data. This book starts from the other end. It takes the mathematics first (groups and their representations, manifolds and their curvature, graphs and their spectra, geodesics, bundles and connections) and derives the architectures from it, proving the results that justify them rather than quoting them.

I wrote it because it was the book I wanted to read and could not find. The survey that named the field (Bronstein et al., 2021) sets out the programme with great clarity, but a programme is not a proof, and the proofs are scattered across papers written for specialists in a dozen subfields. Gathering them, stating them in a single notation and filling the gaps between them is the work this book does. It grew out of my final-year project in mathematics at the Universidad Nacional de Educación a Distancia; the mathematical spine is that project, and the rest is what I learned while trying to make it stand on its own.

## Who it is for

Three kinds of readers. Mathematicians who know the tools and want to see what deep learning does with them will find the architectures explained in their own language, with the domain and the symmetry group stated before the layer. Machine learning practitioners who use these architectures and want to understand why they work will find the proofs behind the design rules they already follow. Graduate students entering the field will find, I hope, a single place from which the research literature becomes readable.

## Prerequisites

Linear algebra and multivariable calculus are assumed throughout, as is some comfort with reading proofs. Elementary point-set topology and the vocabulary of measure theory help in Chapter 2, where the universal approximation theorem is proved in full, but both are recalled where they are used. Everything else is developed inside the book: group and representation theory, differential geometry, harmonic analysis and the rudiments of algebraic topology are built from their definitions in Chapter 3, and the longer proofs that would interrupt the main text are collected in Appendix A. No prior exposure to deep learning is required; Chapter 2 starts from the single neuron.

## How to read it

The chapters build on one another in the order shown in Figure 1.2. Chapter 1 sets out the problem. Chapter 2 covers classical networks and their limitations. Chapter 3 is the core: the five Gs (geometry, groups, graphs, geodesics and gauges) and the message passing framework that unifies everything that follows. Chapter 4 and Chapter 5 apply that framework to the two families of models that dominate practice, convolutions and attention, and can be read independently of each other. Chapter 6 closes with what has been shown, what remains open and where the field is heading.

A reader with a mathematics background can skip most of Chapter 2 on a first pass and return to the universal approximation theorem (Section 2.5.3) when it is invoked. A reader interested mainly in graphs and molecules can go from Chapter 3 to the group convolution and permutation sections of Chapter 4 and to the graph attention section of Chapter 5. A reader interested in transformers can go from Chapter 3 straight to Chapter 5.

## Conventions

Definitions, theorems, lemmas, propositions, corollaries, examples and remarks share a single counter within each chapter, so that a reference such as Theorem 3.12 is found between Definition 3.11 and Example 3.13. A table of notation precedes the first chapter; a glossary and a list of acronyms follow the appendix. The short code listings in Chapter 4 and Chapter 5 are there to be read rather than run: they show how a formula becomes a layer. References are cited by author and year and listed alphabetically at the end.

## Acknowledgements

This book would not have been possible without the people who have been by my side since long before its first page existed.

To my father and my mother, for their unwavering support and for always providing me with the means to keep learning, without ever asking what for. This book is, to a large extent, the fruit of that trust.

To my lifelong friends, who have always been there. They have had the patience to hear about groups, graphs and manifolds more often than anyone should, and the generosity to stay when studying took time away from everything else.

To the artificial intelligence models that accompanied me throughout the writing. Their help was not confined to this book: they were patient and tireless study companions during the years in which I learned mathematics from home while holding down a job, answering questions at any hour and pointing out mistakes that would otherwise have gone unnoticed. Any that remain are mine alone.

## Glossary

## Notation

Throughout this book we use the following mathematical notation. Since the book spans multiple areas (functional analysis, algebra, topology, differential geometry, and deep learning), some symbols admit several meanings depending on the context (for example, G may denote a group or a graph, K a convolutional kernel or a key matrix). In general, the surrounding mathematical context determines the correct interpretation of each symbol.

## Chapter 1

## Introduction

Artificial intelligence has experienced exponential growth in recent years, not only in terms of scientific research but as a tool that is rapidly being introduced into people’s everyday lives. The impact and the trend are clear, and we may well be facing one of the most significant changes in the history of technology.

The history of machine learning dates back to the 1940s–1950s, with the first attempts to create computational models inspired by the human brain. The perceptron, proposed by Frank Rosenblatt in 1957 (Rosenblatt, 1958), represented one of the first machine learning algorithms capable of classifying linearly separable patterns. However, the theoretical limitations of the perceptron (formally proven by Minsky and Papert) led to the first “artificial intelligence winter”, a prolonged period of skepticism and reduced funding in the field.

The resurgence came in the 1980s with the development of the backpropagation algo rithm (backpropagation) (Rumelhart et al., 1986) by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams, which made it possible to train multilayer neural networks efficiently. Nevertheless, problems such as the vanishing gradient and the limited computational capacity of the time kept these techniques in the background during the following decades.

The revolution that transformed the field is due to what we now know as deep learning or Deep Learning (DL). The turning point occurred in 2012 with the victory of AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012) in the ImageNet competition, drastically reducing the classification error relative to traditional methods. This success was made possible by the convergence of three factors: large amounts of available data, accessible specialized hardware such as Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) that allowed models with millions of parameters to be trained, and new training techniques that overcame the historical problems of deep networks.

From that moment on, DL has demonstrated its effectiveness in a wide range of tasks: image recognition with superhuman accuracy, natural language processing, content generation, and protein structure prediction, among many others. However, the architectures responsible for these achievements (convolutional, recurrent, and attention networks) were conceived to operate on data organized in regular Euclidean domains: pixel grids, temporal sequences, feature tables. As the research community began to apply these techniques to data with intrinsically richer structure (molecules, social networks, three-dimensional surfaces), it became evident that the assumption of Euclidean regularity constituted a fundamental limitation, not merely technical but conceptual. This realization prompted the emergence of a new paradigm, Geometric Deep Learning (GDL), which proposes inverting the traditional relationship between data and architecture: instead of forcing the data to fit into preexisting models, it is the geometric properties of the data that must dictate the structure of the model.

## 1.1 Limitations of traditional methods

The traditional architectures of Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and DL, especially Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) (which we will study in Chapter 4), Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) networks, and attention models (Chapter 5), have been designed specifically to operate on data with regular Euclidean structure. CNN take advantage of the regular grid structure of images, where each pixel has a fixed number of neighbors at predefined positions. Similarly, RNN and attention models process sequences in which there is a natural temporal order and a linear structure.

This dependence on regular Euclidean structures presents fundamental limitations when the data do not conform to these paradigms. Consider the problem of analyzing social networks: users and their connections form an irregular graph where each node can have an arbitrary number of neighbors, and there is no natural ordering or grid structure. Attempting to apply CNNs directly would require transforming the graph into a Euclidean representation (such as an adjacency matrix), losing crucial structural information and introducing a large number of zeros that make the process computationally inefficient.

Another paradigmatic example is the analysis of molecules in drug discovery. Molecules are naturally represented as graphs where atoms are nodes and chemical bonds are edges. The three-dimensional geometry of the molecule, the chemical properties of the atoms, and the topology of the bonds determine its pharmacological properties. Traditional methods required the manual extraction of specific chemical features (molecular descriptors) or conversion to string representations (such as SMILES), losing three-dimensional geometric information that is crucial for understanding biological activity.

The “curse of non-Euclideanity” also manifests itself in domains such as 3D shape analysis, where the surfaces of objects do not have a natural parameterization on a regular grid. Traditional techniques required voxelization (conversion to a regular 3D grid) or projections onto multiple 2D views, introducing artifacts and losing fine geometric information. This loss of information translates into suboptimal representations that limit the performance of models and require more complex architectures to compensate for representational deficiencies.

Figure 1.1 illustrates these three fundamental categories of data: Euclidean data with a regular grid structure, graphs with irregular topology, and manifolds with continuous geometry.

## 1.2 Geometric Deep Learning

GDL arises as a natural and mathematically rigorous response to the inherent limitations of traditional Deep Learning methods. Instead of adapting the data to existing architectures —a process that invariably introduces information loss and artifacts— this paradigm inverts the relationship: it designs architectures that respect and exploit the intrinsic geometric structure of the data.

The fundamental principle of GDL lies in the recognition that many real-world data domains possess symmetries and natural geometric structure that can be exploited to improve both computational efficiency and predictive performance. By incorporating these symmetries directly into the neural architecture, GDL not only solves representation problems but also guarantees desirable properties such as equivariance, robust generalization, and efficiency in the use of parameters.

![](images/page_26_image_2.jpg)

Figure 1.1: Comparison of the three fundamental types of data according to their geometric structure: Euclidean data with a regular grid structure (left), graphs with irregular topology where each node can have a different number of neighbors (center), and manifolds with continuous geometry that require local parameterizations (right).

The complete mathematical foundations of GDL, including group theory, the concepts of equivariance and invariance, and the unifying framework of the “5 Gs”, will be developed in depth in Chapter 3 after establishing the foundations of artificial neural networks in Chapter 2. For now, it is sufficient to understand that GDL provides a theoretical framework that unifies seemingly disparate architectures such as convolutional networks, graph networks, and attention mechanisms under a common geometric paradigm. Table 1.1 presents a summary of these five fundamental concepts.

Table 1.1: The five Gs of Geometric Deep Learning

| Concept | Description | Example in GDL |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Geometry | Intrinsic structure of the data domain | Molecule as a 3D graph embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ |
| Groups | Symmetries that preserve the structure of the problem | Rotations SO(3), permutations $S_{n}$ |
| Graphs | Discretizations of geometric domains that capture neighborhood relations | Social network as a graph of users |
| Geodesics | Optimal paths that determine the propagation of information | Message passing in GNNs |
| Gauges | Local invariances in the choice of coordinate systems | Local frames in 3D meshes |

## 1.2.1 Applications and Success Stories of GDL

Computational biology constitutes one of the fields where GDL has had a more profound impact. Molecules are, naturally, three-dimensional graphs whose nodes represent atoms and whose edges encode chemical bonds; Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) exploit this structure to predict pharmacological properties directly from the topology and geometry of the molecular graph, overcoming the limitations of classical chemical descriptors. AlphaFold (Jumper et al., 2021) paradigmatically illustrates the power of this approach: by means of networks equivariant under the Euclidean group E(3), it managed to solve the problem of predicting the three-dimensional structure of proteins, a challenge that had remained open for decades in structural biology. Its successor, AlphaFold 3 (Abramson et al., 2024), abandoned the SE(3)-equivariant structure module in favour of a diffusion model that operates directly on atomic coordinates and recovers the symmetry only through data augmentation with random rotations and translations, while generative models on Lie groups, such as SE(3) diffusion for protein backbones (Yim et al., 2023), have become central to protein design; the tension between built-in equivariance and scale that this contrast reveals is examined in Section 4.7.4, and generative modelling on manifolds and Lie groups is discussed in Section 6.3.3. On the other hand, social network analysis and recommendation systems take advantage of graph architectures to capture complex relationships between users and content in irregular topologies, where invariance to permutations of the set of nodes is the relevant symmetry.

In three-dimensional vision and computational physics, GDL makes it possible to process the native geometric domains of the data directly. Point clouds and polygonal meshes are processed without resorting to voxelization or projections onto multiple two-dimensional views, thus preserving the fine geometric information of the surfaces. In physical simulation, equivariant networks operate on irregular meshes and respect the symmetries of the partial differential equations that govern the system, which makes it possible to obtain physically consistent predictions with greater efficiency than classical numerical methods.

Beyond these consolidated domains, GDL is opening up lines of research in interdis ciplinary fields where the geometric structure of the data plays a fundamental role. In computational neuroscience, graph networks model brain connectivity (both structural and functional) and make it possible to identify patterns associated with neurological disorders that tabular methods do not detect. In materials science, the crystallographic symmetries of solids are encoded into equivariant networks to predict the mechanical, thermal, and electronic properties of new compounds. Climatology takes advantage of the spherical geometry of the Earth to build weather prediction models by means of spherical CNNs that respect the symmetries of the group SO(3). In finance, transaction networks are represented as temporal graphs whose topology evolves and where GNNs detect patterns of fraud or systemic risk. This diversity of applications makes it clear that geometry is not a technical detail specific to each domain, but the common organizing principle that GDL identifies and formalizes.

## 1.3 Objectives of the book

The main objective of this book is to provide a rigorous mathematical formalization of GDL, establishing the theoretical foundations that unify modern deep learning architectures. To achieve this general objective, the following specific objectives are proposed:

1. **Theoretical foundations**: Develop the mathematical framework of the “5 Gs” (Geometry, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, Gauges) that structure GDL, providing the necessary foundations of group theory, differential geometry, and harmonic analysis.

2. **Architectural unification**: Formally demonstrate how seemingly disparate architectures (CNNs, GNNs, Transformer Architectures (Transformers)) emerge as particular cases of the geometric paradigm, connected by the principle of equivariant message passing.

3. **Geometric extensions**: Analyze the extensions of traditional operations (convolutions, attention mechanisms) to non-Euclidean domains, showing how the symmetries and equivariances present in the data can be exploited to improve the performance and efficiency of models.

4. **Theory–architecture connection**: Illustrate, through the analysis of concrete architectures, how the formalized geometric principles manifest themselves in modern models, connecting the theory with representative architectures of GDL.

This book is theoretical in nature, with an emphasis on the mathematical rigor of the definitions, proofs, and formal connections among the various frameworks presented.

## 1.4 Structure of the Document

This book is structured following a logical progression from the theoretical foundations to the advanced models of GDL. Figure 1.2 shows the map of dependencies among chapters.

![](images/page_28_image_8.jpg)

Figure 1.2: Structure and dependencies among the chapters of the book.

The content of each chapter is briefly described below:

**Chapter 2: Artificial Neural Networks** - The foundations of classical artificial neural networks are established, including the perceptron model, universal approximation theorems, and the inherent limitations of Euclidean approaches that motivate the development of the unifying geometric framework.

**Chapter 3: Geometric Deep Learning: A Unifying Theoretical Framework** - The fundamental theoretical framework that unifies all neural architectures under geometric principles is developed. The chapter presents the “5 Gs” (Geometry, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, Gauges), the mathematical foundations of equivariance and invariance, and demonstrates how ANNs, CNNs, GNNs, and Transformers emerge as special cases of a general geometric paradigm.

**Chapter 4: Convolutional Models** - An exhaustive exploration of the geometric extensions of traditional CNNs is presented. The chapter covers everything from the foundations of group theory and equivariance to advanced implementations including Group-Equivariant Convolutional Neural Networks (G-CNNs) for finite groups, Steerable CNNs for SO(2), spherical CNNs for SO(3), gauge convolutions, and algebraic extensions based on Clifford algebras. Rigorous mathematical analyses, implementation algorithms, and connections with theoretical physics are included.

**Chapter 5: Attention Models** - A unified perspective on attention mechanisms is developed from the framework of geometric deep learning. The chapter integrates group theory, spectral analysis, differential geometry, and algebraic topology to mathematically ground Transformers and their extensions. Recent developments such as Geometric Algebra Transformerss (GATrs), attention on manifolds, advanced topological algebra with the Hodge Laplacian and persistent homology, as well as applications in the sciences, are included.

**Chapter 6: Conclusions** - The book closes by gathering what the geometric route has shown: how the five Gs reduce the differences between architectures to three choices, and how one operator reproduces them all. It then states the limitations that the theory itself exposes (the Weisfeiler-Leman barrier, the tension between rigidity and adaptability, global topology, higher-order structures) and surveys where the field is going, from hybrid architectures and generative models on manifolds to the prospects for a unified theory.

**Main Contributions of this Book:** This book provides a **rigorous mathematical formalization** of the fundamental principles of Geometric Deep Learning, establishing the **formal connections** among seemingly disparate architectures (ANNs, CNNs, GNNs, and Transformers) under a unifying geometric framework, and providing a **unified theoretical analysis** that demonstrates how these architectures emerge as instances of a common geometric paradigm.

## Chapter 2

# Artificial Neural Networks

Artificial neural networks (ANN) represent one of the earliest and most successful approaches to biologically inspired computation. Their development began in 1943 when Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts proposed the first formal mathematical model of an artificial neuron (McCulloch and Pitts, 1943), establishing the conceptual foundations that endure to this day.

The central motivation of ANN is to emulate, in a simplified manner, the information processing of biological neurons. These specialized cells receive input signals, integrate them through complex electrochemical processes, and generate output responses that propagate through interconnected networks. Crucially, biological neurons exhibit synaptic plasticity, adapting their responses based on experience and enabling learning from examples.

This analogy with the processing mechanisms of the human brain has motivated decades of research in artificial intelligence, seeking to develop computational systems capable of learning and adapting in a manner similar to biological systems. In this chapter we will examine the mathematical foundations of ANN, from the individual neuron to modern deep architectures.

## 2.1 Artificial Neuron

![](images/page_30_image_6.jpg)

Figure 2.1: Diagram of a biological neuron showing dendrites (inputs), soma (cell body), and axon (output). This structure inspired the McCulloch-Pitts mathematical model.

The McCulloch-Pitts model established the conceptual foundations by abstracting the behavior of a biological neuron (Figure 2.1) into simple mathematical terms. In the nervous system, neurons receive electrochemical signals from other cells through dendrites and synaptic connections. These signals are integrated in the cell soma, and if the weighted sum exceeds a critical depolarization threshold, the neuron generates an action potential that propagates through the axon toward other neurons.

Inspired by this mechanism, an artificial neuron constitutes a mathematical model that:

1. Receives multiple numerical input signals

2. Weights them through adjustable parameters (synaptic weights)

3. Applies a nonlinear activation function that models the firing threshold

4. Produces an output signal that can serve as input to other neurons

It is important to recognize that real biological neurons exhibit a complexity that goes far beyond this initial abstraction. Neuronal processes involve complex temporal dynamics, specific chemical neurotransmitters, time-dependent synaptic plasticity, and intricate three-dimensional dendritic architectures. Nevertheless, the simplification of the McCulloch-Pitts model has proved to be extraordinarily fruitful, providing the conceptual basis for the development of modern ANN.

## 2.1.1 Mathematical formulation

The standard mathematical model of an artificial neuron can be formulated as a function that maps an input vector $\begin{aligned} { \mathbf { x } = ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) ^ { T } } \\ \end{aligned}$ to a scalar output y. The fundamental operation consists of:

$$
y = \sigma \left(\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} w _ {i} x _ {i} + b\right)\tag{2.1}
$$

where:

$\begin{aligned} { \mathbf { w } = } & { { } ~ ( w _ { 1 } , w _ { 2 } , \ldots , w _ { n } ) ^ { T } } \\ \end{aligned}$ are the synaptic weights that modulate the importance of each input

• b is the bias or activation threshold

• σ is the nonlinear activation function

The activation function σ plays a fundamental role by introducing the essential nonlinearity that allows neural networks to approximate complex functions and capture nonlinear relationships in the data. The synaptic weights w and the bias b constitute the adjustable parameters of the model. These are updated during the training process to approximate the desired target function.

## Spiking Neural Networks

It is important to mention that this classical formulation, although extremely successful, represents a simplified abstraction of neuronal behavior. There exist alternative models that are closer to biology, such as **Spiking Neural Networks** or Spiking Neural Network (SNN), considered the “third generation” of neural networks (Maass, 1997). Unlike the classical model where the output is a continuous value, SNNs process information through discrete pulses (spikes) that propagate over time, thus capturing the temporal dynamics inherent to biological neurons. These networks use models such as Integrate-and-Fire or Hodgkin-Huxley, where the neuron accumulates membrane potential until reaching a threshold and emitting a spike. SNNs offer significant computational advantages in terms of energy efficiency and are especially promising for neuromorphic hardware (Tavanaei et al., 2019). However, for the purposes of this book, we will focus on the classical artificial neuron model described above.

## Formal definition

To establish a rigorous mathematical framework for this book, we first formalize the concept of activation function and, subsequently, that of artificial neuron.

**Definition 2.1** (Activation function). An activation function is a function $\sigma : \mathbb { R } \rightarrow \mathbb { R }$ that satisfies the following properties:

• **Nonlinearity**: σ is not an affine map,

• **Continuity**: $\sigma$ is continuous,

• **Differentiability almost everywhere**: $\sigma$ is differentiable except possibly on a set of Lebesgue measure zero<sup>1</sup>.

These properties ensure that σ can introduce the nonlinearities necessary for the expressive capacity of the network, while allowing the computation of gradients for training through backpropagation. Table 2.1 summarizes the main activation functions used in practice along with their most relevant properties, and Section 2.3.4 describes each of them in detail.

**Definition 2.2** (Artificial neuron). Let $n \in \mathbb { N }$ and let $\sigma : \mathbb { R } \rightarrow \mathbb { R }$ be an activation function. For each $\theta = \dot { ( \mathbf { w } , b ) } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n + 1 }$ with $\mathbf { w } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ (weights) and $b \in \mathbb { R }$ (bias), an artificial neuron is a function $f _ { \theta } : \mathbb { R } ^ { n } \to \mathbb { R }$ expressed as the composition of an affine map with an activation function:

$$
f _ {\theta} (\mathbf {x}) = \sigma \circ T _ {\theta} (\mathbf {x}) = \sigma \Big (\langle \mathbf {w}, \mathbf {x} \rangle + b \Big)\tag{2.2}
$$

where $T _ { \theta } : \mathbb { R } ^ { n } \to \mathbb { R }$ is the affine map defined by

$$
T _ {\theta} (\mathbf {x}) = \langle \mathbf {w}, \mathbf {x} \rangle + b.
$$

The set of parameters θ is trainable, which means that during the learning process it is adjusted to minimize a loss function. Thus, an artificial neuron defines a family of functions $\{ f _ { \theta } : \theta \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n + 1 } \}$ parameterized by the weights and the bias.

Figure 2.2 illustrates the structure of an artificial neuron, showing the flow from the weighted inputs to the activated output.

The nonlinearity of σ is crucial: the composition of multiple affine maps remains an affine map, so that without nonlinear activation functions, a deep neural network with multiple layers would be equivalent to a single linear transformation, losing all its expressive capacity. It is this nonlinearity that allows neural networks to approximate arbitrarily complex functions, as established by the universal approximation Theorem 2.94 (see Section 2.5.3).

<small><span class="docvortex-page-footnote" data-block-type="page_footnote" style="color:#6b7280">1<sub>A</sub> set A ⊂ R has Lebesgue measure zero if it can be covered by intervals whose total length is arbitrarily small. See Definitions 2.75 and 2.78 for the formal definition.</span></small>

**Inputs**

![](images/page_33_image_3.jpg)

Figure 2.2: Structure of an artificial neuron. The inputs $x _ { i }$ are multiplied by weights $w _ { i }$ summed together with the bias $b ,$ and the result $\textstyle z = \sum w _ { i } x _ { i } + b$ is transformed by the activation function $\sigma$ to produce the output $y = \sigma ( z )$

## Desirable properties of activation functions

Although 2.1 establishes the minimum properties necessary for a function to serve as an activation function, in practice it is desirable that it satisfy additional properties that facilitate training and improve the behavior of neural networks. Below we present a detailed analysis of these desirable properties.

**Definition 2.3** (Boundedness or controlled growth). An activation function $\sigma : \mathbb { R } \rightarrow \mathbb { R }$ has controlled growth if it satisfies one of the following conditions:

1. **Boundedness**: There exists $M > 0$ such that $| \sigma ( z ) | \leq M$ for all $z \in \mathbb { R }$

2. **Linear growth**: There exist constants $C _ { 1 } , C _ { 2 } > 0$ such that $| \sigma ( z ) | \leq C _ { 1 } | z | + C _ { 2 }$ for all $z \in \mathbb { R }$

This property is crucial for numerical stability during training. The first condition (boundedness) guarantees that activations remain within a finite range regardless of the magnitude of the input, preventing any numerical overflow. The second condition (linear growth) is more permissive: it allows activations to grow, but at a rate no greater than that of the input itself. In both cases, the explosion of values during forward propagation is prevented, which otherwise could cause numerical overflows or excessively large gradients. Table 2.1 shows that the usual activation functions satisfy one or the other condition; for detailed descriptions of each function, see Section 2.3.4.

**Definition 2.4** (Monotonicity). A function $\sigma : \mathbb { R } \rightarrow \mathbb { R }$ is monotonic (increasing) if for any $z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { R }$ with $z _ { 1 } < z _ { 2 }$ it holds that:

$$
\sigma (z _ {1}) \leq \sigma (z _ {2})
$$

Monotonicity provides three fundamental advantages:

1. **Order preservation**: Activations maintain the relative order of the inputs, facilitating interpretability.

2. **Uniqueness of local optima**: In combination with convexity of the loss function, it simplifies the optimization landscape.

3. **Smoothness of the loss surface**: It reduces the presence of spurious local minima in the parameter space.

Most classical activation functions are monotonic (see Section 2.3.4). However, monotonicity is not a necessary condition for good empirical performance: there exist non-monotonic activation functions that exhibit competitive results in practice, which suggests that the theoretical advantages of monotonicity may be offset by other favorable properties.

**Definition 2.5** (Zero-centered). An activation function $\sigma : \mathbb { R } \rightarrow \mathbb { R }$ is zero-centered if it satisfies:

$$
1. \sigma (0) = 0 \text {or} \sigma (0) \approx 0
$$

2. It is symmetric with respect to the origin: $\sigma ( - z ) = - \sigma ( z )$ for all $z \in \mathbb { R }$ (odd function)

This property significantly accelerates the convergence of training. When activations are zero-centered, the gradients have a mean close to zero, which avoids systematic biases in the weight updates.

When an activation function does not satisfy this property (for example, if its range is not centered at the origin, if $\sigma ( 0 ) \neq 0 )$ , the outputs of each layer present a systematic bias. This causes all the gradients with respect to the weights of the same layer to have the same sign, causing the “zigzagging” phenomenon during gradient descent: the parameter updates oscillate between orthogonal directions instead of converging directly toward the optimum.

**Definition 2.6** (Non-saturating gradient). An activation function $\sigma   :   \mathbb { R }   \rightarrow   \mathbb { R }$ has a non-saturating gradient if there exists $\delta > 0$ and a set $S \subseteq \mathbb { R }$ of infinite measure such that:

$$
| \sigma^ {\prime} (z) | \geq \delta \quad \text {for all} z \in S
$$

This property is fundamental to avoid the vanishing gradient problem, one of the main obstacles in training deep networks (see the formal analysis in Section 2.5.2).

**Corollary 2.7.** Every bounded activation function with horizontal asymptotes necessarily saturates.

Proof. If lim $_ { \cdot z \rightarrow \pm \infty }   \sigma ( z ) = c _ { \pm }$ with $c _ { + } , c _ { - }$ finite, then lim $\scriptstyle \operatorname { t } _ { z \to \pm \infty } \sigma ^ { \prime } ( z ) = 0$ . For any $\delta > 0$ there exists $M > 0$ such that $| \sigma ^ { \prime } ( z ) |   <   \delta$ for all $| z | > M$ , so that the set $\{ z : | \sigma ^ { \prime } ( z ) | \geq$ $\delta \} \subseteq [ - M , M ]$ has finite measure. By 2.6, σ cannot have a non-saturating gradient and, therefore, necessarily saturates. □

When $| z |$ is large, $| \sigma ^ { \prime } ( z ) | \approx 0$ , which causes the gradients to become exponentially small in deep layers during backpropagation. Mathematically, if we consider a network with L layers where each layer has a saturated activation, the gradient of the loss with respect to the weights of the first layers will be proportional to $\textstyle \prod _ { \ell = 1 } ^ { L } \sigma ^ { \prime } ( z ^ { ( \ell ) } )$ , which can become numerically zero.

A function that maintains $| \sigma ^ { \prime } ( z ) | \geq \delta > 0$ on a set of infinite measure allows the gradient to flow without attenuation through multiple layers. The optimal case corresponds to functions whose derivative is constant equal to 1 on a half-line, which completely eliminates saturation in that active region and facilitates the training of very deep networks. Moreover, if one requires $| \sigma ^ { \prime } ( z ) | > 0$ for all $z \in \mathbb { R }$ (that is, a strictly nonzero gradient over the entire domain), the risk that certain neurons stop contributing to learning (a phenomenon known as “dead neurons”) is eliminated.

Figure 2.13 (see Section 2.5.2) visually illustrates how the gradient vanishes exponentially in deep networks with saturating activations, compared to the stable behavior of non-saturating activations.

**Definition 2.8** (Computational efficiency). An activation function is computationally $e f f i c i e n t$ if both $\sigma ( z )$ and its derivative $\sigma ^ { \prime } ( z )$ can be evaluated in $O ( 1 )$ time with basic arithmetic operations.

In deep neural networks with millions of neurons, the activation function is evaluated billions of times during training. Therefore, its computational efficiency has a direct impact on the total training time.

Taxonomy by type of operation:

• **Comparisons and selections** (functions defined piecewise through max): They require only comparison and selection operations, which makes them extremely efficient on modern hardware.

• **Transcendental functions** (exponentials, logarithms): They are evaluated in $O ( 1 )$ but with a significantly larger constant than the previous ones, as they require internal polynomial approximations.

• **Vector functions** (normalization over the entire output vector): They have $O ( n )$ complexity in the dimension of the vector, since they require computing global statistics before normalizing each component.

Although all these categories are polynomial in complexity, the differences in constants are significant in practice. The computationally simplest activation functions allow deeper networks to be trained in less time, which has been a relevant factor in the widespread adoption of comparison-based activations.

**Definition 2.9** (Lipschitz continuity). A function $\sigma : \mathbb { R } \rightarrow \mathbb { R }$ is Lipschitz continuous if there exists a constant $L > 0$ (called the Lipschitz constant) such that for any $z _ { 1 } , z _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { R } ;$

$$
| \sigma (z _ {1}) - \sigma (z _ {2}) | \leq L | z _ {1} - z _ {2} |
$$

Lipschitz continuity is stronger than uniform continuity and provides quantitative control over how perturbations in the input propagate to the output. This has certain advantages in the training of neural networks:

1. **Numerical stability**: Small changes in the weights produce bounded changes in the activations.

2. **Gradient control**: If σ is Lipschitz with constant L, then $| \sigma ^ { \prime } ( z ) |   \leq   L$ almost everywhere (where the derivative exists).

3. **Convergence guarantees**: Many convergence theorems for optimization algorithms assume Lipschitz continuity of the objective function.

For activation functions that are differentiable almost everywhere, the Lipschitz constant can be computed as $L = \operatorname { s u p } _ { z } | \sigma ^ { \prime } ( z ) |$ . Bounded functions with horizontal asymptotes tend to have small Lipschitz constants (since their derivative vanishes at the extremes and reaches a moderate maximum), while functions with linear growth typically present $L = 1$ Table 2.1 collects the concrete values for the most common activation functions.

It should be noted that a function can be Lipschitz continuous without being of class $C ^ { 1 }$ it suffices that it be continuous and have a bounded derivative almost everywhere. At points of non-differentiability, subgradients are used, which is sufficient for the gradient-based optimization algorithms employed in the training of neural networks.

The properties presented are not mutually exclusive, and the most successful activation functions in practice usually combine several of them. Table 2.1 summarizes the properties of the most widely used activation functions.

Table 2.1: Comparison of common activation functions

| Function | Formula | Range | Centered | Non-saturating | Lipschitz |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sigmoid | 1+1e-z | (0,1) | No | No | L= 14 |
| Tanh | e<sub>e</sub><sup>zz</sup>-+ee--<sup>z</sup>z | (-1,1) | Yes | No | L=1 |
| ReLU | max(0,z) | [0,∞) | No | Yes (z >0) | L=1 |
| Leaky ReLU | max(αz,z) | R | No | Yes | L=1 |
| Swish | z·σ(z) | ≈(-0.3,∞) | No | Partial | L≈1.1 |

Figure 2.3 graphically shows the most common activation functions together with their derivatives, allowing one to visualize the saturation zones and the behavior of the gradient.

A fundamental theoretical result that justifies the use of activation functions with these properties is the **universal approximation theorem** (see Section 2.5.3), which establishes that neural networks with a single hidden layer and appropriate activation functions can approximate any continuous function on a compact set with arbitrary precision. This theorem will be presented and proved in detail later in this chapter, together with the functional analysis preliminaries necessary for its complete understanding.

The choice of the appropriate activation function depends on the specific problem, the network architecture, and practical training considerations. In the following sections we will see how these properties influence architecture design.

## 2.2 Data and its structure

In the previous section we defined the artificial neuron as a function that processes input data and generates output data. However, in this formulation we have not spoken about the information or the data that the neural network processes; we have not stopped to think about what the space $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ really represents. It is necessary to understand whether the data in the space $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ are simply numbers or whether there is some kind of relationship between them that contains relevant information.

This distinction is crucial. When we represent a $2 8 \times 2 8$ pixel image as a vector in $\mathbb { R } ^ { 7 8 4 }$ we are not dealing with 784 independent values: each component corresponds to a specific pixel in a two-dimensional grid, and spatially neighboring pixels are naturally related. The grid structure is not arbitrary, but intrinsic to the nature of the image.

In this section we will formalize this distinction through two complementary conceptual frameworks that will allow us to unify the treatment of classical Euclidean data (vectors, images, sequences) with complex geometric data (graphs, manifolds, point clouds). In the following subsections we will present two mathematically equivalent frameworks but

![](images/page_37_chart_2.jpg)

![](images/page_37_chart_3.jpg)

![](images/page_37_chart_4.jpg)

![](images/page_37_chart_5.jpg)

Figure 2.3: Common activation functions and their derivatives. The shaded zones indicate regions of saturation where the gradient tends to zero. Note how ReLU maintains a constant gradient for $z > 0 .$ , while Sigmoid and Tanh saturate at the extremes.

with distinct conceptual emphases: the domain-structure-signal triple $( \Omega , \mathcal { S } , f )$ and the geometry-attributes pair $( { \mathcal { D } } , f )$

## 2.2.1 Signals over structured domains

The first conceptual framework is based on three fundamental components that clearly separate the notions of positions, relations, and values. This tripartite decomposition constitutes the basis of the unifying paradigm of GDL developed in Chapter 3, where the “five $\mathrm { G ^ { \prime } s ^ { \prime \prime } }$ of Bronstein et al. (2017) (geometry, groups, graphs, geodesics, and gauges) extend and enrich these fundamental concepts.

**Definition 2.10** (Data domain). A data domain is a set Ω whose elements represent the positions or locations where the data are observed. It can be:

• **Discrete and finite**: $\Omega   =   \{ p _ { 1 } , \ldots , p _ { n } \}$ (vertices of a graph, pixels of an image, indices of a vector)

• **Discrete and infinite**: $\Omega = \mathbb { Z } ^ { d }$ (infinite grid)

• **Continuous**: $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ or a differentiable manifold M

**Definition 2.11** (Domain structure). The structure $\mathcal { S }$ over a domain Ω defines the intrinsic relations between its elements. It can be of a:

• **Topological** nature: A topology τ that defines open sets and notions of neighborhood

• **Metric** nature: A distance function d : $\Omega \times \Omega \to \mathbb { R } _ { \geq 0 }$ that quantifies separations between points

• **Algebraic** nature: Symmetries represented through a group G that acts on Ω

• **Combinatorial** nature: A graph $( V , E )$ that defines explicit connections between points

• **Geometric** nature: A differentiable manifold with atlas, Riemannian metric, connection, etc.

The pair (Ω, S) constitutes a structured domain.

Each type of structure over the domain corresponds to a branch of mathematics that provides specific tools for its analysis. In Chapter 3 we will delve deeper into these structures and into how the symmetries of the domain (formalized through groups) determine the equivariance constraints that neural architectures must satisfy.

**Definition 2.12** (Signal). A signal over a structured domain $( \Omega , S )$ is a function

$$
f: \Omega \to \mathcal {C}
$$

that assigns to each point $p \in \Omega \mathrm { ~ a ~ }$ feature vector $f ( p ) \in { \mathcal { C } }$ , where C is a vector space called the channel space. Typically $\mathcal { C } = \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , where d is the number of channels or attributes.

When Ω is finite, $\Omega = \{ p _ { 1 } , \ldots , p _ { n } \}$ , and $\mathcal { C } = \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , we can represent the signal through the matrix:

$$
F = \left[ \begin{array}{c} f (p _ {1}) ^ {T} \\ f (p _ {2}) ^ {T} \\ \vdots \\ f (p _ {n}) ^ {T} \end{array} \right] \in \mathbb {R} ^ {n \times d}
$$

where each row $f ( p _ { i } ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ contains the features observed at the position $p _ { i }$ .

**Remark 2.13.** The choice of $\mathcal { C } = \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ is sufficient for most of the applications we will treat in this chapter. However, in later chapters the channel space acquires a richer structure: in Chapter $3 , \mathcal { C }$ can be a representation space of a symmetry group $G$ (for example, spherical harmonics for $S O ( 3 ) )$ , and in the context of gauge-equivariant networks, $\mathcal { C }$ corresponds to the fiber of an associated vector bundle over the base manifold.

**Definition 2.14** (Signal space). Given a structured domain $( \Omega , S )$ and a channel space ${ \mathcal { C } } ,$ the signal space $\mathcal { F } ( \Omega , \mathcal { C } )$ is the set of all signals over Ω with values in $\mathcal { C } ;$

$$
\mathcal {F} (\Omega , \mathcal {C}) = \{f: \Omega \to \mathcal {C} \}.
$$

When Ω is finite with $| \Omega |   =   n$ and $\mathcal { C } = \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ , the signal space is isomorphic to a matrix space: $\mathcal { F } ( \Omega , \mathbb { R } ^ { d } ) \cong \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times \overset { \cdot } { d } }$ , where each signal is identified with its matrix representation $F .$ When Ω is continuous, the space $\mathcal { F } ( \Omega , \mathcal { C } )$ is restricted to a function space with appropriate regularity conditions (for example, $\dot { [ } L ^ { 2 } ( \dot { \Omega } , \mathcal { C } )$ or $C ^ { k } ( \Omega , \mathcal { C } ) )$

A neural network can then be viewed as an operator between signal spaces. A layer transforms input signals into output signals, possibly over different domains and channel spaces:

$$
T: \mathcal {F} (\Omega , \mathcal {C}) \to \mathcal {F} (\Omega^ {\prime}, \mathcal {C} ^ {\prime}).
$$

This functional perspective will be fundamental in the chapters on convolutional networks (Chapter 4), where convolution is an equivariant linear operator between signal spaces, and on attention mechanisms (Chapter 5), where attention implements an adaptive nonlinear operator.

In summary:

• The **domain** Ω: defines where the data are (the positions)

• The **structure** $\mathcal { S } ;$ defines how the positions relate to one another

• The **signal** $f ;$ defines the observed values at each position

Figure 2.4 visually illustrates this conceptual framework and how the three components combine to form complete data.

![](images/page_39_image_14.jpg)

Figure 2.4: Conceptual framework for the representation of data. The domain Ω defines the positions, the structure $\mathcal { S }$ defines the relations between positions, and the signal $f$ assigns values to each position. Together they form the complete data that a neural network processes.

A vector $\mathbf { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ is not merely a collection of n real numbers: it represents a signal $f$ over a domain $\Omega$ with a specific structure S. The relations between components $x _ { i }$ and $x _ { j }$ are not arbitrary, but are determined by the structure of the underlying domain.

**Example 2.15** (Audio signal (temporal)). Let us consider an audio signal represented formally as:

• **Domain**: $\Omega = [ 0 , T ] \subset \mathbb { R }$ (continuous temporal interval)

• **Structure**: S = total order of R with the standard topology

• **Signal**: $f ( t ) \in \mathbb { R }$ (sound amplitude at instant t)

At each time instant t, we observe an amplitude f(t). The structure is the temporal order: $t _ { 1 }   <   t _ { 2 }$ has causal meaning. Audio signals respect temporal locality: values at nearby instants are typically correlated.

**Example 2.16** (Digital image on a grid). A digital image is structured as:

• **Domain**: $\Omega = \{ 1 , \ldots , H \} \times \{ 1 , \ldots , W \}$

• **Structure**: S = rectangular 2D grid with local neighborhood (4- or 8-connected)

• **Signal**: $f ( i , j ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$ (RGB intensities of pixel $( i , j ) )$

If we arbitrarily permute the order of pixels when vectorizing the image, the vector representation changes, but the image (as a signal over a 2D grid) remains invariant. The grid structure is intrinsic to the geometric object, not to its particular vector representation.

**Example 2.17** (Social network (graph)). A social network is modeled through:

• **Domain**: $\Omega = V = \{ u _ { 1 } , \ldots , u _ { n } \}$ (set of users)

• **Structure**: $\mathcal { S } = ( V , E )$ where $E \subseteq V \times V$ represents connections or friendships

• **Signal**: $f ( u ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ (profile of user u: age, interests, activity, etc.)

There is no canonical order of users. The “position” of a user is not a numerical index, but its abstract identity in the graph. The relations are defined by the edges E, not by the proximity of indices in some arbitrary vectorization. Two users $u _ { i } , u _ { j }$ are “neighbors” if and only if $( u _ { i } , u _ { j } ) \in E$

**Example 2.18** (Molecule (3D geometric graph)). A molecule combines discrete structure and continuous geometry:

• **Domain**: $\Omega = \{ a _ { 1 } , \ldots , a _ { n } \}$ (set of atoms)

• **Structure**: $\mathcal { S } = ( \mathrm { g r a p h }$ of chemical bonds) + (positions in R<sup>3</sup>) + (symmetries under the Euclidean group $E ( 3 )$

• **Signal**: $f ( a ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ (atomic type, partial charge, atomic mass, hybridization, etc.)

The molecule combines discrete connectivity (covalent chemical bonds) with continuous geometry (three-dimensional positions of atoms). The physicochemical properties are invariant under transformations of the Euclidean group $E ( 3 )$ : translations, rotations, and reflections do not change the molecular identity.

**Example 2.19** (3D point cloud). A three-dimensional point cloud is characterized by:

• **Domain**: $\Omega = \{ p _ { 1 } , \ldots , p _ { n } \} \subset \mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$ (finite set of points in space)

• **Structure**: $\mathcal { S } = \mathrm { E u c l i d e a n }$ metric $d ( p _ { i } , p _ { j } ) = \| p _ { i } - p _ { j } \| _ { 2 }$ • **Signal**: $f ( p ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ (surface normals, curvatures, colors, reflectance, LIDAR intensity, etc.)

There is no natural order of the points. Permuting the list $\{ p _ { 1 } , \ldots , p _ { n } \}$ does not change the point cloud as a three-dimensional geometric object. The structure is purely metric: only the relative distances between points matter, not their order of enumeration.

**Example 2.20** (3D surface (Riemannian manifold)). A 3D surface as a Riemannian manifold is defined through:

• **Domain**: $\Omega = \mathcal { M }$ (2D differentiable manifold embedded in $\mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$ , for example, the surface of a protein or a 3D object)

• **Structure**: S = Riemannian metric g induced by the embedding in $\mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$

• **Signal**: $f   :   \mathcal { M }   \rightarrow   \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ (scalar or vector fields over the surface: temperature, hydrophilicity, Gaussian curvature, etc.)

The geodesic distances over M and the curvature are intrinsic properties of the manifold, independent of the particular embedding in $\mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$ . Two different parameterizations of the same surface define the same intrinsic geometry.

**Example 2.21** (Text sequence (NLP)). A text sequence for natural language processing is represented as:

• **Domain**: $\Omega = \{ 1 , 2 , \ldots , L \}$ (discrete positions in a sequence of length L)

• **Structure**: S = total order with bidirectional sequential structure (each position i can attend to previous and subsequent positions)

• **Signal**: $f ( i ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ (vector embedding of the token at position i: semantic representation of words, subwords, or characters)

Unlike one-dimensional audio with strict causality, text allows bidirectional dependencies: the meaning of a word depends on both the preceding and the subsequent context. Transformer architectures exploit this structure through attention mechanisms that allow each position to interact with all the others, respecting permutation invariance except for the positional encodings that preserve the sequential order.

**Remark 2.22** (Permutation invariance). The previous examples reveal a fundamental distinction. In some domains (audio, text, image) there exists a canonical or partial order of the positions, so that the matrix representation $F   \in   \mathbb { R } ^ { n \times d }$ is essentially unique. In others (graphs, point clouds), no such order exists: if $P \in \{ 0 , 1 \} ^ { n \times n }$ is a permutation matrix, then F and P F represent the same signal over the same domain, simply with the positions enumerated in a different order. Formally, the signal $f : \Omega \to { \mathcal { C } }$ is intrinsic to the domain, but its matrix representation depends on an arbitrary choice of enumeration $\Omega = \{ p _ { 1 } , \ldots , p _ { n } \}$

This observation has profound consequences for the design of neural architectures: a network that processes data without a canonical order must produce results that are invariant (for classification tasks) or equivariant (for per-node prediction tasks) under permutations of the input. This is one of the central ideas of GDL that we will formalize in Chapter 3.

Table 2.2 summarizes the characteristics of the previous examples, highlighting the diversity of domains and the presence or absence of a canonical order.

Table 2.2: Comparative summary of the examples of signals over structured domains. The column “Canonical order?” indicates whether the positions of the domain have a natural ordering, which determines whether the matrix representation is unique up to permutations.

| Example | Ω | Type ofS | dim(C) | Order? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Audio | [0,T] | Total order | 1 | Yes |
| Image | 2D grid | Rectangular grid | 3 (RGB) | Yes (partial) |
| Social network | Vertices | Graph | d | No |
| Molecule | Atoms | Graph +E(3) | d | No |
| 3D cloud | Points ⊂R<sup>3</sup> | Euclidean metric | d | No |
| Surface | M | Riemannian | d | No |
| Text | {1,...,L} | Sequential | d | Yes |

## 2.2.2 Geometry and attributes

The previous framework separates domain, structure, and signal into three distinct components. However, it can be conceptually useful to unify the domain and its structure into a single entity: the geometry of the problem.

**Definition 2.23** (Domain geometry). The geometry of a data problem is the pair $\mathcal { D } = ( \Omega , \mathcal { S } )$ that combines the domain Ω with its structure S into a single entity that completely characterizes the spatial, topological, or algebraic relations between positions.

**Definition 2.24** (Attributes). The attributes (or features) are the image, the signal $f : \Omega \to { \mathcal { C } }$ that assigns observed values to each position of the domain.

The two conceptual frameworks are mathematically equivalent. The equivalence is direct: $( \Omega , \mathcal { S } , f ) \leftrightarrow ( \mathcal { D } , f )$ where $\mathcal { D } = ( \Omega , \mathcal { S } )$

The geometry/attributes framework offers an important conceptual advantage by distinguishing between intrinsic structure and variable observations:

• The **geometry** $\mathcal { D } = ( \Omega , \mathcal { S } )$ is typically fixed or intrinsic to the individual datum: it defines the “shape” of the data space.

• The **attributes** f are variable: different data instances share the same geometry but have different attributes.

This distinction is fundamental for the design of neural architectures: the operations must respect the geometry (which is intrinsic) while transforming the attributes (which are variable). Ignoring the geometry, as a simple neuron does with a global inner product, wastes valuable structural information.

## 2.2.3 Neural processing of signals

Having established the framework of signals over structured domains, we can now reinterpret the artificial neuron defined earlier and analyze its limitations from a geometric perspective.

An artificial neuron $f _ { \theta } : \mathbb { R } ^ { n } \to \mathbb { R }$ can be reinterpreted as an operator that processes signals over a discrete domain:

• **Input domain**: $\Omega = \{ 1 , 2 , \ldots , n \}$ (finite set of indices with no particular geometric meaning)

• **Structure**: None significant (set without geometric, topological, or algebraic relations)

• **Input signal**: $x : \Omega \to \mathbb { R }$ where $x ( i ) = x _ { i }$ represents the value at index i

• **Processing**: $\begin{array} { r } { y = \sigma ( \langle \mathbf { w } , \mathbf { x } \rangle + b ) = \sigma \left( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } w _ { i } \cdot x ( i ) + b \right) } \end{array}$

The linear transformation $\begin{array} { r } { \langle \mathbf { w } , \mathbf { x } \rangle = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } w _ { i } x _ { i } } \end{array}$ combines all the components globally through a weighted sum. There is no notion of:

• **Locality**: All positions $i \in \Omega$ contribute equally to the output; there is no concept of “local processing” based on neighborhood

• **Structured neighborhood**: No distinction is made between “nearby” and “distant” indices; the connection $w _ { 1 } x _ { 1 }$ has the same structural character as $w _ { 1 0 0 } x _ { 1 }$ <sub>0</sub>0

• **Geometric invariance**: Permuting the indices through $\pi : \{ 1 , \ldots , n \} \to \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ produces a different signal $x _ { \pi }$ where $x _ { \pi } ( i ) = x ( \pi ( i ) )$ , and typically $f _ { \theta } ( x _ { \pi } ) \neq f _ { \theta } ( x )$ even though semantically the permutation may be irrelevant (for example, in graphs)

The neuron treats the domain $\Omega = \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ as a set without structure, ignoring any geometry that may exist implicitly in the nature of the data.

ANNs focus on transformations of the signal or attributes between layers, leaving the geometry in the background, or using it solely to optimize computational calculations. In GDL we will see that the geometry of the data takes on greater relevance and is one of the fundamental pillars. The concrete examples of different types of geometries (Euclidean, of graphs, manifolds) and their relationship with neural architectures are developed in depth in the Geometric Deep Learning chapter (Chapter 3), where the complete mathematical framework is presented.

## 2.3 Layers of a neural network

In 2.2, we presented an artificial neuron as a function with a single scalar output:

$$
f (x) = \sigma (w ^ {T} x + b): \mathbb {R} ^ {n} \to \mathbb {R}
$$

This choice is not arbitrary, but responds to several criteria:

1. **Biological analogy**: Biological neurons emit a single output signal (firing rate), which propagates through the axon toward other neurons. The scalar definition captures this fundamental characteristic.

2. **Mathematical simplicity**: A function $\mathbb { R } ^ { n } \to \mathbb { R }$ is conceptually simpler than a function $\mathbb { R } ^ { n } \rightarrow \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ , facilitating the initial analysis of the properties of an individual neuron (separation by hyperplane, nonlinear activation, etc.).

Mathematically, we could have defined a neuron as a vector function $f : \mathbb { R } ^ { n } \to \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ with multiple outputs. However, this generalization does not provide additional expressive power: a neuron with m outputs is functionally equivalent to m scalar neurons operating in parallel, each with its own weights and bias. Therefore, we adopt the scalar definition as the primitive, and we will build more complex architectures through the composition and parallelization of these basic units.

To obtain multiple output values, we use several neurons that share the same input domain. Each neuron independently transforms the input signal into a single scalar value, and the set of the m outputs forms a new signal that, in general, resides over a domain different from the input that may have a different structure. This organization leads us to formalize the notion of a neural layer.

**Definition 2.25** (Neural layer). A neural layer is a set of m neurons that share the same input domain and operate in parallel over the input signal. Given an input signal $\mathbf { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ (where n is the dimension of the input domain), the layer produces an output signal $\mathbf { y } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ through:

$$
L (\mathbf {x}) = \sigma (\mathbf {W} \mathbf {x} + \mathbf {b})
$$

where:

$\mathbf { W } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m \times n }$ is the weight matrix, whose i-th row contains the weights $w _ { i } ^ { T }$ of neuron i

• b $\in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is the bias vector

$\sigma$ is the activation function, applied component-wise

Each neuron $i$ computes $y _ { i } = \sigma ( w _ { i } ^ { T } \mathbf { x } + b _ { i } )$ , transforming the attributes of the input signal into a single output attribute.

**Connectivity and sparse matrices.** The matrix representation $\mathbf { W } \mathbf { x } + \mathbf { b }$ is completely general. If a neuron i only processes a subset of the positions of the input domain, this is expressed through zero coefficients: $W _ { i j } = 0$ when neuron i does not receive a signal from position $j .$ Although in practical implementations optimizations for sparse matrices are used, mathematically every neural layer admits this unified representation. This observation will be relevant when we study architectures with structured connectivity, such as convolutional networks.

**Shared weights.** 2.25 assumes that each neuron has its own independent parameters $( w _ { i } , b _ { i } )$ . However, in many architectures the weights are shared between neurons: multiple rows of the matrix W contain the same values. Mathematically, this imposes constraints of the form $W _ { i , : } = W _ { j , }$ : for certain pairs $( i , j )$ , drastically reducing the number of free parameters.

## 2.3.1 Composition of layers

A neuron by itself is not capable of solving complex problems, but by combining many of them into a network one can learn more complex functions. As we have seen in 2.2, a neuron is a function of the form $\textstyle y = \sigma \left( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } w _ { i } x _ { i } + b \right)$ , where $\sigma$ is a nonlinear activation function. Geometrically, the linear part $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } w _ { i } x _ { i }   +   b$ defines a hyperplane in $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ , and the activation function introduces a nonlinearity that transforms this hyperplane. An individual neuron, therefore, can only separate the input space through a single nonlinearly transformed hyperplane. This drastically limits its expressive capacity: it cannot approximate functions with multiple complex decision regions, hierarchical patterns, or highly nonlinear structures. For example, an individual neuron cannot solve the classic XOR problem, which requires a non-linearly-separable partition of the space.

When we connect multiple neurons organized into layers, we obtain a function composition of nonlinear transformations. We will denote by $L _ { i }$ the i-th layer of the network, where each layer $L _ { i } : \mathbb { R } ^ { n _ { i - 1 } } \to \mathbb { R } ^ { n _ { i } }$ transforms a signal of dimension $n _ { i - 1 }$ into a signal of dimension $n _ { i }$ . A neural network of k layers computes the composition:

$$
\mathcal {N} = L _ {k} \circ L _ {k - 1} \circ \dots \circ L _ {2} \circ L _ {1}: \mathbb {R} ^ {n _ {0}} \to \mathbb {R} ^ {n _ {k}}
$$

where $n _ { 0 }$ is the dimension of the input domain and $n _ { k }$ that of the output domain.

This composition has fundamental mathematical properties:

1. **Hierarchical representations**: Each composition $L _ { i } \circ L _ { i - 1 } \circ \cdots \circ L _ { 1 }$ can be interpreted as a transformation that extracts increasingly abstract features from the data. The first layers detect simple patterns (edges, textures), while later layers combine these patterns into representations of higher semantic level (shapes, objects).

2. **Complex partitioning of the space**: Multiple neurons in a layer generate multiple hyperplanes, allowing $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ to be partitioned into arbitrarily complex polyhedral regions. The composition of layers recursively refines these partitions, creating highly nonlinear decision boundaries.

![](images/page_45_image_8.jpg)

Figure 2.5: Structure of a feedforward neural network organized into layers. The nodes represent individual neurons with colors differentiated by type of layer: input (blue), hidden (green/teal/violet), and output (orange). The arrows represent weighted connections $w _ { i j } ^ { ( \ell ) }$

In an ANN we have a first layer of the network called the input layer that receives the raw data, that is, the signal of the problem domain; and the last layer is the output layer that produces the final response of the network. The intermediate layers are known as hidden layers, since they are not directly seen at the input or the output of the neural network.

Let us look in more detail at why it is important to have more than one layer and more than one neuron in some layer, in the XOR problem.

## The XOR problem

The XOR problem consists of computing the logical function:

$$
\mathrm{XOR} (x _ {1}, x _ {2}) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & \text {if exactly one input is 1} \\ 0 & \text {otherwise} \end{array} \right.
$$

This problem is not linearly separable: there is no single hyperplane that separates the classes (0, 0), (1, 1) (output 0) from (0, 1), (1, 0) (output 1) in $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$

![](images/page_46_image_2.jpg)

Figure 2.6: Geometric solution of the XOR problem through two neurons. Each neuron of the hidden layer defines a hyperplane $( h _ { 1 }$ and $h _ { 2 } )$ that divides the space. The region between the two hyperplanes corresponds to XOR=1 (red points), while the outer regions correspond to $\mathrm { X O R { = } 0 }$ (blue points).

Figure 2.6 geometrically illustrates how two neurons in the hidden layer, each defining a hyperplane, allow the XOR problem to be solved.

Which architectures can solve XOR?

• **1 layer with 1 neuron**: Impossible. A neuron computes $\sigma ( w _ { 1 } x _ { 1 } + w _ { 2 } x _ { 2 } + b )$ , which defines a single hyperplane. XOR requires a non-convex decision boundary.

• **Many layers with 1 neuron each**: Also impossible. If each layer applies a scalar function $f _ { i } : \mathbb { R } \to \mathbb { R }$ , the composition $f _ { k } \circ \dots \circ f _ { 1 } : \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } \to \mathbb { R }$ collapses all the twodimensional information to a scalar immediately, losing the ability to distinguish the four regions of the input space.

• **2 layers with** {2, 1} **neurons**: Sufficient. The hidden layer with 2 neurons creates two hyperplanes that partition $\mathbb { R } ^ { \tilde { 2 } }$ into regions, and the output neuron linearly combines these partitions to generate the XOR boundary.

This counterexample reveals that neither width alone nor depth alone suffices: we need $m \geq 2$ neurons in at least one layer and at least $k \geq 2$ layers. Extreme architectures (deep-narrow or shallow-wide with $m = 1 )$ fail on fundamental problems.

## 2.3.2 Width vs depth

The analysis of the XOR problem leads us to formalize two fundamental concepts that characterize the architecture of a neural network: width and depth. These parameters determine the expressive capacity of the network and have profound implications, both theoretical and practical.

**Definition 2.26** (Width of a layer). The width of a layer $L _ { i } : \mathbb { R } ^ { n _ { i - 1 } } \to \mathbb { R } ^ { n _ { i } }$ is the dimension $n _ { i }$ of its output space, that is, the number of neurons it contains.

**Definition 2.27** (Depth of a network). The depth of a neural network $\mathcal { N } = L _ { k } \circ \dots \circ L _ { 1 }$ is the number k of layers in the composition.

These formal definitions allow us to rigorously analyze the balance between width and depth.

Width provides diversity of features: each neuron captures a different aspect of the input signal, and the output signal $h \in \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ simultaneously encodes multiple geometric properties of the datum.

Depth provides hierarchical abstraction: instead of attempting to solve the complete problem at once, each layer performs an intermediate transformation, delegating the final refinement to the subsequent layers. The layers implement a hierarchy of representations where each level extracts features of increasing complexity:

$$
x \xrightarrow {L _ {1}} h ^ {(1)} \xrightarrow {L _ {2}} h ^ {(2)} \xrightarrow {L _ {3}} \dots \xrightarrow {L _ {k}} y
$$

Empirically, it is observed that:

• **Early layers** $( L _ { 1 } , L _ { 2 } )$ : Detect low-level features (edges, textures, basic colors in images; phonemes in audio).

• **Intermediate layers** $( L _ { 3 } , \dots , L _ { k - 2 } )$ : Combine low-level features into more complex patterns (geometric shapes, textural motifs).

• **Final layers** $( L _ { k - 1 } , L _ { k } )$ : Represent high-level concepts specific to the task (objects, scenes; words, semantic concepts).

This hierarchy reflects the compositional structure of many real-world problems and allows the network to learn increasingly abstract and semantically meaningful representations.

As we will see in the Universal Approximation Theorem (Section 2.5.3), neural networks with a single sufficiently wide hidden layer can approximate any continuous function on a compact set with arbitrary precision. However, this existential guarantee does not specify the efficiency of such an approximation in terms of the number of neurons required.

**Approximation theory and depth.** Recent theoretical results demonstrate that depth (number of layers) provides exponential advantages in expressive capacity. For certain classes of functions, a deep network of moderate width can approximate functions that would require an exponentially larger number of neurons if limited to a single layer (Telgarsky, 2016). Mathematically, this is because the composition of functions allows the construction of functions with combinatorial complexity that grows exponentially with depth.

We have seen that, although a single hidden layer suffices theoretically to approximate continuous functions, deep architectures offer exponential advantages in efficiency. In practice, deep networks with different types of specialized layers are preferred, each adapted to specific aspects of the problem, in order to optimize both the expressive capacity and the computational cost. This specialization reflects a fundamental distinction: while some layers transform only the values of the signal preserving its spatial structure, others modify the geometric organization itself of the domain. This functional taxonomy will allow us to better understand the difference between traditional deep learning architectures and the GDL approach.

## 2.3.3 Types of layers

Neural layers can transform the signal, the domain, or both simultaneously. This distinction is fundamental to understand the philosophical and mathematical difference between traditional ANNs and GDL: while the former typically ignore or destroy the original geometry of the datum, the latter preserve and systematically exploit it.

Formally, we classify layers into three categories according to which dimension they transform:

**Definition 2.28** (Pure signal transformation). A layer L is a pure signal transformation if it preserves the structure of the input domain. Formally, if the input is a signal $f : \Omega \to \mathbb { R } ^ { c _ { \mathrm { i n } } }$ the output is $g : \Omega \to \mathbb { R } ^ { c _ { \mathrm { o u t } } }$ where the domain Ω remains invariant.

**Characteristics:**

• Point-wise (element-wise) operations: $g ( x ) = \phi ( f ( x ) )$ for some function $\phi : \mathbb { R } ^ { c _ { \mathrm { i n } } } \rightarrow$ $\mathbb { R } ^ { c _ { \mathrm { o u t } } }$

• Preserve the shape of the input tensor

• Do not require information about neighborhoods, connectivity, or geometric structure

**Definition 2.29** (Pure geometric transformation). A layer L is a pure geometric transformation if it modifies the geometric structure of the domain without processing the values of the signal in a non-trivial way. Formally, if $f : ( \Omega , \mathcal { G } ) \rightarrow \mathbb { R } ^ { c }$ is a signal over a domain Ω with geometric structure $\mathcal { G }$ (metric, connection, topology), then $L ( f ) = g : ( \Omega ^ { \prime } , \mathcal { G } ^ { \prime } ) \to \mathbb { R } ^ { c }$ where the geometry $\mathcal { G } ^ { \prime } \neq \mathcal { G }$ , but the values of the signal are preserved or reindexed according to a correspondence $\pi : \Omega ^ { \prime } \to \Omega$

In **traditional neural networks**, pure geometric transformations typically reduce to reindexings (reshape, transpose, flatten), since the underlying domain is a discretized Euclidean space without rich geometric structure. However, in GDL, these transformations include more sophisticated operations: changes of coordinate system, projections between manifolds, modifications of the metric or connection, and conformal or isometric transformations. The distinction is fundamental: while in traditional ANN the geometry is “flat” and purely structural transformations are trivial, in GDL the geometry is intrinsic to the problem and geometric transformations can be highly non-trivial.

**Definition 2.30** (Coupled signal-geometry transformation). A layer L is a coupled transformation if it simultaneously and intrinsically modifies both the signal and the domain. Formally, $L : \left( f : \Omega \to \mathbb { R } ^ { c _ { \mathrm { i n } } } \right) \mapsto \left( g : \Omega ^ { \prime } \to \mathbb { R } ^ { c _ { \mathrm { o u t } } } \right)$ where typically $\Omega ^ { \prime } \neq \Omega$ and g cannot be expressed as a reindexing of $f .$

**Traditional neural networks** (multilayer perceptrons, dense networks) are based mainly on layers that destroy or completely ignore the original geometry of the datum. It is very typical to flatten the geometry and transform it into a vector, losing all information about spatial neighborhoods and local structure, or not using the intrinsic properties of the geometry such as symmetries to improve neural networks. In contrast, as we will see in Chapter 3, GDL preserves and systematically exploits the underlying geometry.

## 2.3.4 Traditional layers

By way of introduction, we will briefly present here some of the layers traditionally used in Deep Learning.

## Activation functions

Activation functions introduce essential nonlinearities in ANN, allowing them to approximate complex functions. Without these nonlinearities, any neural network would reduce to a simple linear transformation, drastically limiting its expressive capacity. Earlier we saw that the activation function is an intrinsic part of the neuron, but for practical reasons it is usually implemented as an independent layer that transforms the output of each neuron component-wise. We consider this type of layers among those that only perform transformations of the signal.

Below we present the most widely used activation functions, analyzing in each case the desirable properties established in 2.3 (see also Table 2.1 for a summarized comparison):

**Sigmoid** The sigmoid function is one of the classical activation functions. Its range of values is (0, 1), useful for probabilistic interpretations:

$$
\sigma (x) = \frac {1}{1 + e ^ {- x}}
$$

It is bounded (2.3), monotonic (2.4) and Lipschitz continuous with constant $L = 1 / 4$ (2.9). However, it is not zero-centered (2.5), since $\sigma ( z ) \in ( 0 , 1 )$ and $\sigma ( 0 ) = 1 / 2 \neq 0$ , which can cause the zigzagging phenomenon in gradient descent. In addition, its horizontal asymptotes $\left( \operatorname * { l i m } _ { z \rightarrow \pm \infty } \sigma ( z ) \in \{ 0 , 1 \} \right)$ imply gradient saturation at both extremes (2.6).

**Hyperbolic Tangent (tanh)** The tanh function has a range (−1, 1):
